stages.title: A chunk arrives
stages.blurb: Bytes enter through one of three entry points. The parser picks a walk and keeps whatever state is needed to resume mid-token.

stages.title: The dispatcher
stages.blurb: A switch over thirteen states. Each token class is a separate function it calls out to.

stages.title: Whitespace
stages.blurb: One compare in front of the run scan. How much whitespace there is to find is a property of the document, not of JSON.

stages.title: Strings and escapes
stages.blurb: Sixteen bytes per compare, three terminators tested at once. The non-ASCII answer leaves with the end index.

stages.title: Numbers
stages.blurb: A greedy scan finds the token; the narrowest kernel that fits its shape parses it.

stages.title: The sink boundary
stages.blurb: Token-granular, non-throwing, borrowed spans. The boundary between the format-agnostic parser and a destination.

stages.title: Typed routing
stages.blurb: Turning a key into a store. Most of this layer is now data rather than closures.

stages.title: Storage and reading
stages.blurb: Where bytes accumulate, and what reading them before the document ends costs.

nodes.title: parse(_:into:)
prose: Everything starts here. A chunk of bytes goes in, tokens come out the other side into a sink, and the parser keeps whatever state is needed to resume mid-token when the chunk ends somewhere awkward — inside a string, halfway through a number, between the two halves of a surrogate pair.

The entry point itself does almost nothing: it picks a walk and wraps the loop in the handler that flushes to the sink before an error propagates. That ordering matters — everything emitted ahead of a grammar error still belongs to the sink, so a destination that rejected something earlier gets to report *its* failure rather than having the parser's take precedence.

The chunk's address is never stored. It is threaded down into the walk and on into every emission, because the run loop already holds it in a register — and what the parser *does* store is laid out to a cache line, with everything a parse reads or writes in the first sixty-four bytes.

next.label: n ≥ windowThreshold
next.when: The chunk is large enough to index ahead of the walk. `parseWindowed` takes it and `parse` returns without touching the byte loop.

next.label: otherwise
next.when: The ordinary path: the bytes are walked directly by `parseDispatching`, which is force-inlined so the loop's layout is what it was when it lived here.

next.label: on the way out
next.when: Both walks end the same way — `settlePendingStringBegin`, then `commitSink`, then the consumed-byte count advances. This also runs on the error path, which is the point: what was emitted before a grammar error still belongs to the sink.

nodes.invokes: One length test picks the walk, and the whole call is wrapped in a handler that commits to the sink before any error propagates.

steps.title: A call arrives
steps.detail: Two entry points share one state machine: `parse(_:into:)` takes a buffer and `parse(byte:into:)` takes a single byte. Neither reads anything before recording where the bytes are.

next.label: one byte, inside a string
next.when: The shape byte-fed input is mostly made of: an ordinary ASCII byte in a string value. Six tests deep — state, the byte's own range, then three parser fields — and it produces one record without the dispatcher, the scan or the scratch.

next.label: a buffer
next.when: `parse(_:into:)`. An empty buffer returns having touched nothing.

steps.title: deliverStringByte
steps.detail: One `stringChunk` carrying the byte itself, so there is no pointer to take and nothing to store either. Anything that fails one of the six tests falls through to the dispatcher unchanged.

steps.title: the base is a parameter
steps.detail: The chunk's address is handed down into the walk and on into every emission rather than written to a field. `chunkBase` was that field, and it had exactly one reader — the function that builds a token's span — so reading it back there was a load from a cache line the run loop otherwise never touches, while the loop already held the pointer in a register. With the pointer arriving as an argument the span builder is `static`: nothing of the parser is left in the result, and keeping the old `@_lifetime(borrow self)` shape on a body that no longer reads `self` tripped a SIL ownership verifier crash in the `PartialSink` specialisation of the structural run.

steps.title: one cache line of state
steps.detail: Field order here is a cache-line decision, not a taste one. Everything a parse reads or writes lives in the first sixty-four bytes; past them sit `ownsBuffer`, which only the deinit reads, and the window telemetry, which is dead for any parser that never crosses `windowThreshold` — the default. The small fields are narrowed to their real ranges rather than bit-packed: narrowing is free on arm64, where `ldrb`/`ldrh` zero-extend, while packing per-byte state into shared words would turn plain stores into read-modify-writes on the string and unicode paths and break the store fusion the compiler already performs on the adjacent flags — it emits one `strh` for `isKeyToken` and `keyContainsNonASCII`. The buffer is split out of its `UnsafeMutableBufferPointer` so its capacity sits next to the count the append guard compares against: one eight-byte load answers both.

steps.title: n vs windowThreshold
steps.detail: One compare picks the walk. The threshold defaults to `Int.max`, so the windowed path is off unless a caller asks for it.

next.label: n ≥ threshold
next.when: Long enough to be worth indexing 32 KB ahead of the walk.

next.label: n < threshold
next.when: The ordinary path: the dispatcher walks the bytes itself.

steps.title: parseWindowed
steps.detail: The indexed walk. Its own node covers what it does and why it is gated.

steps.title: parseDispatching
steps.detail: The switch-per-state loop that owns every token class.

steps.title: settle, then commit
steps.detail: A pending `stringBegin` is settled and `commit()` reaches the sink *before* a grammar error propagates. Everything emitted ahead of the error is still the sink's, so a destination that rejected something earlier reports its own failure rather than having the parser's take precedence.

next.label: the caller has no more bytes
next.when: `finish()` is a separate call, and the only one that can report a document that ended mid-token.

steps.title: finish()
steps.detail: The state the parser stopped in becomes the verdict: `.number` emits the buffered token, a string state is unterminated, `.literal` is invalid. The lifetime signal goes out before the structural checks, which deliver nothing new.

nodes.title: Chunk boundaries
prose: A chunk boundary can land anywhere, including inside a UTF-8 sequence. The parser holds the incomplete tail in a single 64-bit field — little-endian, a byte per lane — rather than guessing, and completes it against the next chunk's first bytes before the main loop starts.
This is the cost of streaming rather than batching, and it is kept to the edges: the resume path runs once per chunk, not once per byte, so the bulk loop never tests for it.

next.label: resume, then walk
next.when: `completePendingUTF8` finishes the held sequence against the new chunk's first bytes and returns the index the main loop starts from. With nothing held the loop starts at 0 and the test is one compare.

nodes.invokes: Runs once at the top of the next chunk's walk, before the loop starts — never per byte.

steps.title: trimmingIncompleteUTF8
steps.detail: Before a string run that reaches the end of the buffer is emitted, the last four bytes are walked backwards looking for a lead whose sequence the chunk cut. Nothing further back is examined, because no sequence is longer than four bytes.

next.label: a lead is short of its bytes
next.when: The run's last bytes are the head of a sequence this chunk cut, so they are held back instead of emitted.

next.label: the run ends on a whole sequence
next.when: Nothing is pending and the run is emitted as it stands.

steps.title: emit the run
steps.detail: The common case, and the reason this test is where it is: it costs one backwards walk over at most four bytes per run, not per byte.

steps.title: holdPendingUTF8
steps.detail: At most four bytes packed little-endian into one field, a byte per lane, so completion appends at lane `have` with a shift rather than a store. It used to live in the last eight bytes of the parser's buffer — a full page away from everything else the parse touched, and one `buffer.count` subtraction per access. An invalid lead is rejected here rather than held, which leaves completion with only the second-byte constraints left to check.

next.label: carry it into the next chunk

steps.title: completePendingUTF8
steps.detail: Runs once per chunk, ahead of the dispatch loop, so the bulk loop never tests for it. Continuation bytes are taken off the front of the new chunk until the sequence is as long as its lead says.

next.label: the sequence is whole
next.when: Every byte taken was a continuation and the count reached `sequenceLength(lead)`.

next.label: a non-continuation arrived
next.when: The sequence is truncated: `invalidUTF8`, reported at the lead's offset in the *previous* chunk.

next.label: this chunk ran out first
next.when: A sequence can be cut twice by sufficiently small chunks.

steps.title: hold what arrived
steps.detail: The count advances and the rest waits. Byte-fed input takes this arm three times for a four-byte sequence.

steps.title: invalidUTF8
steps.detail: Reported at the lead, which is a negative offset into this chunk: the parser counts consumed bytes, so an error in a sequence the boundary split still names where the sequence began.

steps.title: the second-byte constraints
steps.detail: The fill loop admitted only continuation bytes and the hold rejected invalid leads, so only overlongs, encoded surrogates and scalars past U+10FFFF remain — the same four tests the contiguous validator applies, without its ASCII prescan, which measured 32% of byte-fed non-ASCII throughput.

steps.title: one stringChunk, from the scratch
steps.detail: The rejoined bytes are emitted from an eight-byte scratch the parser reserves past its buffer's capacity rather than from the input, because half of them are in a chunk that no longer exists. The whole word goes out in one unaligned store and the sink is handed a span of the front of it; the high bytes it will not look at are free to write. A sequence rejoined inside a *skipped* string is validated and dropped.

nodes.title: The windowed walk
prose: A large enough chunk can be indexed ahead of the walk, simdjson style: find every structural byte in a 32 KB window first, then walk the index instead of the bytes. The parser will do this, but only above a threshold, and only while the windows stay dense enough to be worth it.

Measured across the full corpus, the windowed walk loses 4–36% on string-heavy and sub-window payloads: the index costs more to build than the walk saves whenever the document is not structurally dense. It is off by default and probes as it goes.

next.label: window not dense enough
next.when: Density is probed per window. When the index stops paying for itself the remaining bytes go through the ordinary dispatch loop, which is also what happens for the whole chunk when the gate is off.

nodes.invokes: Indexes a 32 KB window, walks the index rather than the bytes, and measures density as it goes.

steps.title: one scratch allocation
steps.detail: Held on the parser and reused across calls: 32 KB of `UInt32` positions plus two bitmap planes, one for the blocks that need a scan and one for the blocks holding non-ASCII.

steps.title: is the cursor at a token boundary?
steps.detail: A window may start only outside a string with nothing buffered, because the indexer carries no state across windows. Anything else is the dispatcher's.

next.label: the chunk is consumed
next.when: The walk ends where a bulk parse would, with the same events already delivered.

next.label: mid-token
next.when: Inside a string, a buffered number, an escape in flight: one dispatcher step at a time until the cursor is back at a boundary.

next.label: structural, nothing buffered
next.when: The cursor is at a token boundary outside any string, which is the only state the indexer can be started from.

steps.title: one dispatcher step
steps.detail: The same handler the bulk path would have run, so the sink cannot tell which walk produced the events.

steps.title: windowDensity vs 3
steps.detail: Entries per 64 bytes, measured on the last window that was indexed. Census: llm_message 0.7 and gsoc-2018 2.1 against citm 6.0, github 6.4, twitter 7.4 and canada 9.5.

next.label: below 3, probed recently
next.when: String interior with little structure: the index costs more to build than the walk saves, so the span is the dispatcher's.

next.label: dense, or every eighth window
next.when: Every eighth window is indexed regardless, so a document that turns dense again is noticed within one window.

steps.title: hand the span to the dispatcher
steps.detail: Bounded by where the steps stop, not by what they scan — a handler may overrun the span, as a string longer than it would — so the sink sees exactly the chunks a bulk parse produces.

steps.title: stream_parsing_index_window
steps.detail: Stage one, in C: every position the walk must visit, written eight slots at a time. The whole loop is across the boundary because the shuffle it needs takes a target attribute Swift cannot spell.

next.label: walk the index, not the bytes

steps.title: consumeWindow
steps.detail: The dispatcher's structural arms restated over known token extents. It still hands back every token a window cuts and every key with an escape in it — both cold — and the cursor comes back short of the window end when it does.

steps.title: consumeObjectMembers
steps.detail: The object arm of the indexed walk: key, colon and value come out of the index rather than from a scan. The index does not promise a scalar directly after a quote an entry of its own, so the gap between a key's closing quote and its colon is checked before either the key is emitted or the colon consumed — compact JSON takes the adjacent-colon compare and never scans whitespace at all. A complete key and colon can also be the last bytes of an incomplete chunk, so the value is left pending before its first byte is inspected; it belongs to the next parse call. Either check failing hands the cursor back to the dispatcher with the state set, rather than guessing.

steps.title: the chunk is consumed
steps.detail: Same events, same spans, same error reasons and offsets, same rejection points as the unwindowed walk. That contract is why the arms are restated rather than rewritten.

nodes.title: parseDispatching
prose: The main loop is a switch over the parser's state that calls out to a handler per token class, and then re-enters. Read on the release binary it is 1284 bytes, 322 instructions, 18 calls and no SIMD at all — a pure dispatcher. Every token class is a separate function: `consumeStructural` at 1044 bytes, `consumeStringRun` at 1204, `consumeNumber` at 928.

Keeping it that way takes explicit attributes, because of register pressure: anything inlined here is paid for by every document, including ones that never execute it. The same state-ladder transformation that made the structural step faster was applied to this loop and measured worse.

next.label: structural states
next.when: `.value`, `.firstValue`, `.afterValue`, `.key`, `.firstKey`, `.afterKey`, `.done` — the states with no token open. They are numbered below the rest so `state.isStructural` is a single unsigned compare.

next.label: .inString / .inKey
next.when: A string body is open. `.inString` streams its bytes; `.inKey` goes to `consumeKeyRun`, which buffers so the key can be delivered whole. `.escape` and `.unicode` are separate arms handled one byte at a time.

next.label: .number
next.when: A number is open. This state is entered when the structural run hands back the byte it stopped on — a number is the one token whose first byte belongs to the token itself.

next.label: .skipping …
next.when: The sink declined this subtree. Three states, all placed past `.done` in the enum so that adding them did not cost everyone else the single-compare structural test.

nodes.invokes: A `switch` on `self.state` at the top of `while i < n`. Exactly one arm runs per iteration; each returns the index it stopped at and the switch runs again, so control comes back here after every run until the chunk is consumed.

steps.title: pending UTF-8 first
steps.detail: Once per chunk, before the loop: a sequence the previous chunk cut is rejoined here so the loop below never has to test for one.

steps.title: switch self.state
steps.detail: Thirteen cases over one `UInt8`, lowered as a jump table. Exactly one arm runs per iteration and each returns the new cursor. Read on the release binary the whole function is 1284 bytes, 322 instructions, 18 calls and no SIMD at all.

next.label: the seven structural states
next.when: `value`, `firstValue`, `afterValue`, `key`, `firstKey`, `afterKey`, `done` share one arm.

next.label: inString / inKey
next.when: A string value and a key take different arms because one is delivered as a borrowed span and the other is buffered.

next.label: escape / unicode
next.when: One byte per call: an escape selector, or one of the four hex digits.

next.label: number / literal
next.when: A token the run handed back, or one a chunk cut.

next.label: the three skipping states
next.when: Past `done` in the enum on purpose, so `isStructural` stays one unsigned compare.

steps.title: consumeStructuralRun
steps.detail: 1044 bytes of `consumeStructural` folded into a run loop.

steps.title: consumeStringRun / consumeKeyRun
steps.detail: 1204 bytes. Every token class is its own function precisely so this loop is not.

steps.title: escape, then hex digits
steps.detail: `consumeEscape` and `consumeUnicodeDigit`: the cold spellings, kept for the escape a chunk boundary cuts and for the ones carrying diagnostics.

steps.title: consumeNumber / consumeLiteral
steps.detail: 928 bytes for the number arm.

steps.title: consumeSkipRun
steps.detail: Structural-speed scanning with no events but the matching close.

steps.title: test i < n
steps.detail: The register pressure argument lives here: anything inlined into this loop is paid for by every document, including the ones that never execute it. The same state-ladder transformation that made the structural step faster was applied to this loop and measured worse.

next.label: the cursor reached n
next.when: The chunk is spent; whatever state the parser is in is what the next call resumes from.

steps.title: return to the caller
steps.detail: No state is reset. The parser resuming mid-token is the whole point of the thing.

nodes.title: The structural run
prose: Structural bytes arrive in runs — `},{"`, `":`, `,"`, `[[` — and paying a call, a return and a re-entry into the dispatch switch for each one was measurably the cost of a structural byte, not the byte's own work. So the loop stays inside one function while the state stays structural, turning a run into a single call.

The register trick is the part worth watching. Nesting is held in two values: `depth`, and a single `UInt64` where bit *n* is 1 if the container at depth *n* is an object and 0 if it is an array. Sixty-four levels of JSON nesting, one register. Depth beyond that is rejected rather than spilled, which is why the ceiling exists at all.

`state`, `depth` and `containers` are copied into locals for the duration of the run and written back on every exit. Left as fields they lived in memory — the release build stored `state` at the end of one byte and loaded it back at the start of the next, and that store-to-load round trip, not the switch, was the loop-carried dependency.

On arm64, a structural boundary with 64 bytes ahead first enters a block walk. The scalar copy is still the edge path and the authority for anything the classifier declines; splitting the two loop copies with `@_transparent` measured neutral on the scalar path.

next.label: 64 bytes ahead, gate open
next.when: On arm64, the parser is at a token boundary with no token in flight and the block walk has not given up on this payload's shape.

next.label: edge or scalar handoff
next.when: Fewer than 64 bytes remain, a block contains something the classifier declines, or a token crosses the grid in a form the block path hands back. `streamWhitespaceEndByte` resumes at exactly that byte.

next.label: then one byte
next.when: `consumeStructural`, folded in `@_transparent`, advances `state`, `depth` and `containers`. All three are locals for the duration of the run and are written back on every exit, the throwing ones included.

nodes.invokes: At the top of each structural-loop iteration, the arm64 copy tries a 64-byte block. The same loop then owns the scalar edge: whitespace scan, state ladder, and another turn until the state stops being structural.

steps.title: copy state, depth and containers into locals
steps.detail: Written back by a `defer` on every exit. Left as fields the release build stored `state` at the end of one byte and loaded it back at the start of the next, and that store-to-load round trip — not the switch — was the loop-carried dependency.

steps.title: is a whole block available?
steps.detail: The block verdict is read once at the function entry; at each token boundary, 64 remaining bytes choose the block walk. The byte-fed and short-tail path reaches the scalar scan without paying for the classifier.

next.label: 64 bytes remain
next.when: The parser is at a structural boundary and the block gate has not given up.

next.label: scalar edge
next.when: The tail is short, the architecture has no block path, or this parse already accumulated four gate strikes.

steps.title: consumeStructuralBlocks
steps.detail: Classifies a block, walks `starts` with trailing-zero counts, and returns the first byte it will not settle. A negative result is the complemented cursor and permanently selects the scalar copy for the rest of this parse.

next.label: state became non-structural
next.when: A string, number or skipped subtree needs its dispatcher arm.

next.label: hands back one byte
next.when: The block path declines at a byte but leaves a structural state for the unchanged scalar loop.

steps.title: streamWhitespaceEndByte
steps.detail: The scan hands back the byte it stopped on as well as the index, so the ladder below reads a register instead of loading the address the scan's one-compare path just tested. Two L1 accesses per structural byte became one.

next.label: i reached the chunk end
next.when: Only whitespace was left; the run returns and the next chunk resumes at the same state.

next.label: a byte
next.when: There is a structural byte at the cursor, and the scan has already handed it over in a register.

steps.title: consumeStructural
steps.detail: One byte, folded in by force. Its own node covers the ladder; what matters here is the three ways it can end a run.

next.label: the byte starts a number
next.when: A number is the one token whose first byte belongs to the token itself, so the ladder returns true, the cursor steps back onto the byte and the run ends.

next.label: the state stopped being structural
next.when: `isStructural` is one unsigned compare on the raw value. A string, key, literal or skip state ends the run and the dispatcher picks the handler.

steps.title: containers |= 1 << depth
steps.detail: Nesting is two values: `depth`, and one `UInt64` where bit *n* is 1 if the container at depth *n* is an object and 0 if it is an array. Sixty-four levels in one register — which is why depth beyond that is rejected rather than spilled.

steps.title: return the cursor
steps.detail: Nothing is written back but the three locals, and the parser resumes at the same state on the next chunk.

steps.title: i -= 1, break
steps.detail: The one place the run deliberately un-consumes a byte.

steps.title: break, and re-dispatch
steps.detail: Paying a call, a return and a re-entry into the dispatch switch per structural byte was measurably the cost of a structural byte, not the byte's own work — which is why this is the *exit* rather than the normal case.

nodes.title: The structural block walk
prose: One C classification replaces the whitespace scan before every token, the string scan before every in-place key or value, and the per-string high-bit reduction. `starts` contains the opening quote or first candidate byte of each token; `quote` pairs string extents; `backslash` decides whether an extent can stay in place.

The grid moves with completed tokens. If a long string or token crosses byte 64, its existing scanner finishes it and the next classification begins at that end rather than at the old fixed boundary. Every classification therefore starts with zero quote and escape carries, and long string interiors are not classified again.

The classifier only pays on shapes where it removes whitespace work. A block with no whitespace outside strings, or at least 48 start candidates, is one strike. Four consecutive strikes store a parser-wide give-up verdict; the unchanged scalar copy handles the rest of that parse.

next.label: the same grammar arms
next.when: The block walk restates the scalar ladder's checks and event order over mask-selected token starts.

next.label: scalar handoff or next turn
next.when: An unsettled byte returns to the scalar edge at its exact offset; exhausted and re-anchored grids return to the structural loop.

nodes.invokes: An outer loop classifies a moving 64-byte grid. An inner loop repeatedly takes `starts.trailingZeroBitCount`, consumes that token extent, and clears every candidate it covered.

steps.title: classify 64 bytes
steps.detail: The C kernel returns `starts`, unescaped quote bits, every backslash bit, the high-byte flag, the scalar-decline flag and the two gate signals. The structural walk always supplies zero carries because it completes every token it starts before moving its grid.

next.label: needs_scalar != 0
next.when: A control byte inside a string or a byte outside strings that the wide path will not judge. The scalar loop re-reads from the block's first byte so errors keep their offsets.

next.label: the block is accepted
next.when: Every byte belongs to a class the block path can settle.

steps.title: update consecutive strikes
steps.detail: No whitespace outside strings or 48+ `starts` bits adds one strike; a useful block resets a nonzero count. Consecutive rather than cumulative preserves the measured GSoC gain across its occasional compact block.

next.label: strike 4
next.when: The walk stores `blockWalkGivenUp` and returns the complemented cursor before visiting this block's starts.

next.label: the gate stays open
next.when: The block remains worth walking, or has not yet accumulated four consecutive losing signals.

steps.title: starts.trailingZeroBitCount
steps.detail: Whitespace and string interiors are absent, so the lowest set bit is the next token candidate after the cursor. There is no whitespace call and no scan across the gap.

next.label: a start bit remains
next.when: The byte itself selects the matching scalar-ladder arm.

next.label: mask == 0
next.when: Every token in the block is finished; anything after the last one is whitespace.

steps.title: settle one token extent
steps.detail: Quotes pair an in-block string immediately; a backslash inside that extent selects the existing escape decoder. Literal words are checked whole. Numbers still use `streamNumberRunEnd`, because only its grammar walk preserves the error byte for shapes such as `12abc`.

next.label: the token ends past byte 63
next.when: The existing token scanner completed a long string, literal or number beyond this grid.

steps.title: p = token end
steps.detail: The next classification begins at the byte after the completed token, with zero carries. The tail of the old grid is abandoned; the token's interior is never classified twice.

next.label: 64 bytes remain at the new p

steps.title: p += 64
steps.detail: The exhausted mask proves no token is open at the edge, so the next block is classified independently.

steps.title: return p unchanged
steps.detail: The block is handed back from its first byte with parser state untouched. The unchanged scalar copy remains the code that diagnoses it.

steps.title: return ~p
steps.detail: The complemented cursor carries the verdict without another mutable local in the structural loop. The dispatcher re-enters once and the entry test selects the scalar copy for the rest of the parse.

nodes.title: The state ladder
prose: One structural byte, folded into the run loop by force. The states are ordered so that "is this still structural" is a single unsigned compare, which is the only reason their numeric values matter.

Two variants of this same code were measured and rejected: reordering the ladder by what the run actually sees, and peeling the colon out of it. A third — the byte ladder — removes strictly more work and is slower. What the four say together is that this function is limited by its size, not by how many times it iterates.

next.label: byte opens a value
next.when: A `"`, a digit, or a literal's first byte. Rather than return to the dispatcher, the run tries to finish the token where it stands.

nodes.invokes: Advances one byte, then answers whether the run continues.

steps.title: a quote, ahead of the ladder
steps.detail: A `"` in a value or key state is scanned here, once, before the ladder. The string scanner is the largest thing inlined into this function, so keys and string values share one copy of it rather than one per arm.

next.label: the closing quote is in this chunk
next.when: No escape before it either: a value becomes one whole `string` record and a key a borrowed span, and the run carries on to the colon or comma.

next.label: the token is cut, or has an escape
next.when: The per-byte path takes the token whole, rescanning from the opening quote. Handing the scanned prefix on instead was built and measured: it returned gsoc-2018's escape-bearing descriptions their 2.5% and cost twitter 2% and Pretty printed users 3–7%.

next.label: not a quote
next.when: Every other structural byte, resolved by which state the parser is in rather than by which byte it is.

steps.title: one record, no state change
steps.detail: Before string values were read here, every value ended the run: `parse` re-dispatched, `consumeStringRun` paid a ten-register prologue, and `fuseAfterValue` handed the comma back — which measured ~25% of the instructions on twitter as transitions rather than token work.

steps.title: leave the run
steps.detail: `stringBeginPending` marks that the opening quote was seen, so the handler records it at the right offset even though the byte is behind the cursor.

steps.title: raw = state.rawValue
steps.detail: A ladder over the raw value rather than a `switch`, which lowers to a jump table: a `leaq`, a `movslq` out of it and an indirect branch per structural byte, with the table's base pinned in a register for the whole run loop. The `State` case order was chosen so the structural pairs are adjacent, which makes each rung one unsigned compare.

next.label: raw ≤ firstValue
next.when: A value is expected.

next.label: raw ≤ firstKey
next.when: Only `}` — closing an object whose keys are done. The quote was taken above.

next.label: raw == afterKey
next.when: The one legal byte is `:`.

next.label: anything else
next.when: `done` is trailing content; the rest is an unexpected token.

steps.title: open, close, literal or number
steps.detail: The widest rung, and the only one that changes depth.

next.label: `{` or `[`
next.when: The disposition the sink answers decides whether the interior is streamed or skipped.

next.label: a literal whole in the chunk
next.when: One 32-bit word compare and an event, finished here so the run carries on to the comma.

next.label: a digit or `-`
next.when: Returns true. The run steps the cursor back and lets `.number` re-read the first byte.

steps.title: depth += 1, containers bit set
steps.detail: The depth cap is checked *after* the sink is told the container opened, so the events stay in the order a streaming sink sees them.

steps.title: one word compare

steps.title: return true
steps.detail: The one rung that ends the run without an error.

steps.title: a comma, or a close
steps.detail: A comma consults the `containers` bit to decide whether a key or a value comes next — one shift and one test, no branch on the container's kind.

steps.title: fuseAfterValue
steps.detail: A token that finished *outside* the run — a buffered string, a number — would otherwise return to the dispatcher just to read the comma. steps.title: `:` and nothing else

steps.title: unexpectedToken

nodes.title: Values finish in the run
prose: A short string value or a literal used to leave the structural run, get handled, and come back. Now they finish in place: the run recognises a complete string or literal and emits it without ever returning to the dispatcher.

steps.title: four bytes, one compare
steps.detail: A literal whole in the chunk is a single 32-bit load against a constant, emitted inside the structural run so the run carries straight on to the comma. This is what the +11.8% on twitter is: transitions that stopped happening.

next.label: the word matched
next.when: One `boolean` or `null` record and the cursor steps over the whole literal.

next.label: the chunk cut it
next.when: Fewer than four or five bytes remain, so the literal cannot be settled here.

steps.title: state = .afterValue
steps.detail: The run never returns to the dispatcher, which is the entire saving. GSoC lost 2.5% to this change; the obvious fix was built, measured, and not kept, because it cost twitter and the pretty-printed payload more than it recovered.

steps.title: startLiteral(kind:)
steps.detail: The kind and an index of 1 — the first byte was already read and matched by the ladder's arm, so only the tail is re-checked.

steps.title: consumeLiteral
steps.detail: One byte per iteration against the expected word. Every literal under byte-fed input takes this path.

next.label: a byte differs
next.when: `invalidLiteral`, reported at that byte.

next.label: the whole word matched
next.when: One record, whose span names only the part of the literal in *this* chunk.

next.label: the chunk ran out first
next.when: `literalIndex` carries how far it got.

steps.title: carry literalIndex
steps.detail: The state survives the chunk boundary; the bytes do not, which is why the record below names a partial span rather than the whole token.

steps.title: invalidLiteral
steps.detail: Reported at the offending byte, not at the start of the literal.

steps.title: one boolean or null record
steps.detail: A literal a chunk began was never read from here, so the record's span covers only what this chunk holds. `extra` carries the boolean's value, so `true` and `false` are one event kind.

nodes.title: One compare, then out of line
prose: This runs before *every* structural byte, and how much whitespace there is to find is a property of the document rather than of JSON: canada has 0%, citm_catalog has 71%, and llm_message has 17% — none of it anywhere this scan can see it, because it is all inside string values.

Every JSON whitespace byte is ≤ 0x20 and every byte that may legally follow one is > 0x20. So a single compare settles the no-whitespace case without touching a vector, and only what survives is scanned SIMD16 like every other class.

What the *inlined body* costs is the whole design constraint here, and it is not the scan. This is forced inline into the parse loop, so anything spelled in it is paid in register pressure by every document. Inlining the vector body gains citm 22% and costs twitterescaped 18% and the unicode-escape payload 35% — for code those documents never execute. Moving it out of line recovers both and keeps the wins.

next.label: byte ≤ 0x20
next.when: The inline compare did not settle it, so there is a real run to scan. Every JSON whitespace byte is ≤ 0x20 and every byte that may legally follow one is > 0x20, so canada (0% whitespace) never reaches here and citm (71%) always does.

nodes.invokes: One compare is spelled inline in the parse loop; everything else stays behind a call, because what the inlined body costs is paid by every document whether or not it has whitespace.

steps.detail: The whole inlined body. Every JSON whitespace byte is ≤ 0x20 and every byte that may legally follow one is > 0x20, so one compare settles the no-whitespace case without touching a vector.

next.when: There is a real run to scan, and everything past this point is behind a call.

steps.title: return `from`
steps.detail: No run, no call, no vector: the cursor is already at the byte the caller wanted.

steps.title: streamWhitespaceEndByte
steps.detail: The same decision, returning the byte it stopped on as well as the index. The reload is spelled out here rather than delegating, so it stays on the cold side of the early return instead of becoming a second exit from a shared tail.

steps.detail: Not a tail guard. Fed one byte at a time, `to - from` is 1 at every call, and routing that through the vector body splats four constants to scan a single byte — which cost byte-by-byte twitter 20%.

next.when: The scalar walk: four compares per byte.

next.label: sixteen or more
next.when: Enough bytes left in the chunk for a full block, so the out-of-line vector body is worth its call.

nodes.title: The run scan
prose: What survives the compare is an actual run, and runs are scanned sixteen bytes at a time like every other token class. The vector body lives behind its own call precisely so the parse loop does not carry it.

There is a width test in front, and it is not a tail guard: fed one byte at a time, `to - from` is 1 at every call, and routing that through the vector body splats four constants to scan a single byte — which cost byte-by-byte Twitter 20%.

next.label: run end + stop byte
next.when: Control returns to the loop that called it, which handles the structural byte and calls back here before the next one. A width test sits in front: fed one byte at a time `to - from` is 1, and routing that through the vector body splats four constants to scan a single byte, which cost byte-by-byte Twitter 20%.

steps.title: two bytes of bitmap test
steps.detail: Exactly two, and written as two rather than as a bounded loop: what this resolves is the one-byte run, which is the median in mesh and canada. Spelled as a loop it did not unroll — eight instructions an iteration plus the bound and the constant, against twelve straight-line for both bytes.

next.label: either byte is not whitespace
next.when: The run was one or two bytes and never reaches the vector body. Widening the peel to four cost citm 3.3% and to eight 10.0%, because citm's runs are long enough that every peeled byte is tax.

next.label: both were whitespace
next.when: The run is at least three bytes, which is the length at which the vector body starts paying: runs of exactly two do not occur, since a separator is one byte and an indent is a newline plus its depth.

steps.title: return i
steps.detail: gsoc +10.9%, Pretty printed users +9.7%, github_events +8.2%, mesh +7.9%, twitter +6.3%, with no row regressing.

steps.title: while i + 16 <= to
steps.detail: The width test in the caller cannot filter these: the bound it reads is the chunk end, not the run end — a scanner cannot know the run end without scanning — so under bulk input every run arrives here.

next.label: a full block remains
next.when: Sixteen bytes are available to load, which is the only condition the loop tests.

next.label: fewer than sixteen bytes left
next.when: The same scalar walk the caller's narrow path uses.

steps.title: load 16, streamWhitespaceMissMask
steps.detail: On arm64 the class test is a `tbl` through a sixteen-entry table indexed by the low nibble, compared against the byte itself: one lookup and one compare where the portable form is four splats, four compares and three ORs.

next.label: a lane missed
next.when: The first lane whose byte is not whitespace is where the run ends.

steps.title: first set lane
steps.detail: The same movemask the string scan uses, so there is one spelling of "which lane" in the whole scanner file.

steps.title: streamWhitespaceScalarEnd
steps.detail: Reached with at most fifteen bytes left, or immediately when the caller's width test routed here.

nodes.title: streamStringRun
prose: Sixteen bytes are loaded, compared against a quote, a backslash and the control-byte floor, and the three results are ORed into one mask. A string run ends at the first lane that hits any of the three; if none do, the block is clean and the scan moves on.

SIMD16 was measured against the alternatives at four run lengths and is fastest at all of them. SWAR is worse than scalar below about 12 bytes and never beats SIMD16; SIMD32 loses on arm64 because NEON registers are 128 bits, so a 32-byte vector lowers to two operations plus a recombine.

The scan also answers a second question. It has already loaded every byte, so it carries out whether any had the high bit set, letting a validated ASCII-only string skip a second pass. The flag is exact rather than conservative: bytes after the terminating lane are masked out before the question is asked.

next.label: how the end is found
next.when: The mask is non-zero, so the run ends at its lowest set lane. Extracting that lane index is the movemask, and its arm64 spelling is what the assembly tab pins.

next.label: the hit was a backslash
next.when: A backslash ends the run and hands control to the escape states, which decode into the destination in place rather than building an intermediate.

next.label: block held a non-ASCII byte
next.when: The scan already loaded every byte, so it carries out whether any had the high bit set. The flag is exact rather than conservative — lanes past the terminating one are masked off before the question is asked — so a clean ASCII run skips validation entirely.

steps.title: first byte against the three terminators
steps.detail: Before any vector setup: a run of length zero is common — an empty string, or the byte right after an escape — and answering it costs one load and three compares against the four splats the body below needs.

next.label: it is one of the three
next.when: The scan returns `from` and the caller reads the terminator itself.

next.label: an ordinary byte
next.when: Not a quote, a backslash or a control byte, so there is a run of at least one byte to scan.

steps.title: return end == from
steps.detail: A SWAR first word was measured in front of this and rejected; so was a 2× unroll of the block loop below.

steps.title: while i + 16 <= narrowLimit
steps.detail: The escalation bound, computed once at entry rather than counted per iteration. A counter incremented and tested inside the loop cost citm 2.6% and the 564-byte Qwen payload 5.0% — documents made of short keys that never reach the wide tier at all. Off x86 the bound is `to` and the whole thing folds away.

next.label: a full block remains
next.when: Sixteen bytes are available below the escalation bound.

next.label: fewer than sixteen bytes left
next.when: The chunk end, or on x86 the escalation bound with no full block behind it.

steps.title: 3 compares, ORed into one mask
steps.detail: `cmeq` against a quote, `cmeq` against a backslash, `cmlo` against the control-byte floor, then two `orr`. SIMD16 was measured against the alternatives at four run lengths and is fastest at all of them: SWAR is worse than scalar below about twelve bytes, and SIMD32 loses on arm64 because NEON registers are 128 bits.

next.label: any lane set
next.when: `any(hit)` is spelled through the shim on arm64: once this body reaches `consumeStructuralRun` the standard library's `any` on a composed mask lost its specialisation and became a call to the generic `SIMD.min`, one `bl` per sixteen string bytes.

next.label: the block is clean
next.when: Sixteen bytes of string content, and the scan moves on.

steps.title: scanned |= chunk
steps.detail: The second question, answered from a load already paid for: whether any byte had the high bit set. A validated ASCII-only string skips UTF-8 validation entirely.

steps.title: mask off the lanes past the hit
steps.detail: `lanes .< lane` selects the bytes *before* the terminator, and only those are ORed into the accumulator. That is what makes the non-ASCII flag exact rather than conservative — a `"` followed by high bytes in the same block does not poison the run that ended before them.

steps.title: streamVectorContainsNonASCII
steps.detail: One `orr`-reduce and a test for any high bit. On arm64 through the shim; elsewhere the vector is reinterpreted as two `UInt64`s, since the high bit of each byte is invariant under that and it avoids the out-of-line `SIMD.min` some `any(mask)` forms produce.

steps.title: byte at a time
steps.detail: At most fifteen bytes, each tested against the same three terminators and contributing to the same flag.

steps.title: StreamStringRun
steps.detail: Two fields out of one pass over the bytes.

next.label: what the caller does with it

steps.title: consumeStringRun
steps.detail: The run is emitted as a `stringChunk` unless it ends the string cleanly, in which case one whole `string` record goes out instead. The hit-path latency chain here was measured — nine dependent operations and a stack spill, both removed — and the parser did not move: +0.07%.

nodes.title: Finding the lane
prose: Once a block hits, the scan needs to know *which* lane. The obvious spelling — loop over sixteen lanes and take the first set one — unrolls into sixteen test/branch pairs plus sixteen constant-materialising exit blocks: over a hundred bytes of branch ladder, walked once per string token and once per key, to produce an integer the machine was already holding.

On arm64 the answer is `vshrn`, which Swift cannot express because its shift is an immediate, so it lives in a C shim. The form that landed fuses the bound check into the lane: an all-ones complement has 64 trailing zeros, which divides to lane 16, one past the block, so the bound check is the terminator test and nothing depends on the branch.

The portable spelling reaches the same answer arithmetically rather than with a select, and the reason is a specific compiler behaviour: written as a ternary, LLVM's x86 cmov-converter turns the intended conditional move back into two branches whenever it judges the condition predictable. On a terminator lane, which is unpredictable by nature, that is exactly wrong.

steps.title: streamMaskBytes
steps.detail: The mask is already sixteen bytes of 0x00 or 0xFF, so the bitcast costs nothing. It exists so both spellings below take the same input and the tests can hold them to one oracle.

next.label: arm64
next.when: The instruction exists, and Swift cannot spell it.

next.label: everywhere else
next.when: No `vshrn`, and no horizontal reduction worth using either.

steps.title: vshrn_n_u16(·, 4)
steps.detail: Sixteen bytes narrowed to eight, four bits per lane, in one instruction. It lives in a C shim because its shift is an immediate, which Swift's SIMD surface has no way to express.

steps.title: trailingZeroBitCount >> 2
steps.detail: The form that landed fuses the bound check into the lane: an all-ones complement has 64 trailing zeros, which divides to lane 16 — one past the block. So `lane` and the branch condition become ready in the same cycle, where testing the mask first leaves `mvn`/`rbit`/`clz` strictly after the branch and a short token pays that chain in full before it can exit.

steps.title: two 64-bit words
steps.detail: The mask reinterpreted as `SIMD2<UInt64>`; each word's trailing zero count is eight lanes' worth of answer.

steps.title: (low >> 3) + ((high >> 3) & lowEmpty)
steps.detail: Arithmetic rather than a conditional move, for a specific compiler reason: written as a ternary, LLVM's x86 cmov-converter turns the intended `cmov` back into two branches whenever it judges the condition predictable. On a terminator lane, which is unpredictable by nature, that is exactly wrong.

nodes.title: Escapes, decoded in place
prose: An escape terminates the run, gets decoded, and the scan resumes. `\uXXXX` sequences are decoded to UTF-8 bytes inside the parser — including surrogate pairs, which have to be held across the gap between the two halves and can be cut by a chunk boundary in the middle.
Nothing here produces a `Unicode.Scalar` or a `String`. That keeps the Unicode data tables out of the binary, which is what lets the core build under Embedded Swift.

steps.title: the run stopped on a backslash
steps.detail: The string scan ends at the backslash and the selector is the next byte. Everything below decides which of two paths reads it.

next.label: `\u` with six bytes left
next.when: Decoded here, in place, so the scan keeps going instead of handing the token to the per-byte states.

next.label: any other selector
next.when: One of the eight one-byte escapes, or an error.

steps.title: consumeEscape
steps.detail: A high surrogate pending here is severed by any escape but a low surrogate, and severing it first is also what keeps the emitted content in order around the error.

next.label: the table has a byte for it
next.when: Written straight into the destination.

next.label: the cell is zero
next.when: `invalidEscape`, reported at the backslash rather than at the selector.

steps.title: streamDecodeSimpleEscape
steps.detail: A byte index into a 128-entry table where zero means "no escape". Exactly eight cells are non-zero, which is the whole of JSON's simple-escape grammar as data rather than as a compare chain.

steps.title: invalidEscape
steps.detail: At `offset - 1`: the backslash, which is where a reader looking at the document would say the escape began.

steps.title: fusedUnicodeEscapeEnd
steps.detail: Outlined, because it is cold relative to the scan it interrupts. The bounds test comes first so the halfword load that follows stays inside the chunk.

next.label: four hex digits
next.when: Six bytes are in the chunk and all four digits parse, so the scalar is known here rather than across four per-byte calls.

next.label: the chunk cut it, or it needs a diagnostic
next.when: A lone low surrogate, or a high surrogate followed by anything but a low one: both are diagnostics, so they go to the per-byte path where the offsets are exact.

steps.title: streamHexQuad
steps.detail: Four bytes at once: the digit range and the letter range tested in parallel, the nibbles selected by mask, then weighted by 0x1000/0x100/0x10/1 and summed. One rejection test covers all four digits.

next.label: a high surrogate
next.when: A pair is twelve bytes and has to be complete and well formed to be fused.

next.label: an ordinary scalar
next.when: Outside both surrogate ranges, so it stands alone.

steps.title: the second escape, in the same call
steps.detail: The `\u` prefix is one halfword compare, then a second `streamHexQuad` and a range test. Only then are the halves combined.

steps.title: consumeUnicodeDigit
steps.detail: One hex digit per call, shifted into `unicodeValue`. A high surrogate is held on the parser across the gap, which is what lets a pair be cut anywhere — including between its two halves.

steps.title: UTF-8 bytes, one store
steps.detail: Nothing here produces a `Unicode.Scalar` or a `String`, which keeps the Unicode data tables out of the binary and is what lets the core build under Embedded Swift. The bytes are assembled little-endian in a register and stored whole — one unaligned eight-byte write into a scratch region the parser reserves past its buffer — and the sink gets a span of the front of it. Storing only the bytes that count, with a loop, measured worse on escape-dense corpora: Twitter escaped bulk 1,289 → 1,374 MB/s for the whole-word form, with every `consumeStringRun` specialisation byte-identical between the two, so the loop is simply not worth its branches. Giving the word its address from a stack local instead cost 10–14%, because the closure materialises it to a fresh slot per escaped byte and captures the sink `inout` across the call.

nodes.title: UTF-8 validation
prose: Non-ASCII content is validated in vectors, using Keiser and Lemire's three-nibble-table construction: three table lookups ANDed together, XORed with a continuation requirement derived from leads two and three bytes back. Nonzero lanes are errors.

The one operation Swift cannot express is the byte table lookup itself — on arm64 that is `tbl`, and it lives in a C shim as a leaf returning a vector. Composing the same kernel from Swift's SIMD primitives instead ran 2.6× slower, because Swift's SIMD operators are lane loops that LLVM re-vectorizes, and a compare feeding a fifteen-lane shift came out half vectorized with the last lanes patched one at a time.
What landed here was not a better kernel but a deferred reduction: hoisting the per-block reduction out of the loop measured +5.7%, while a 2× unroll of the same loop measured no change.

steps.title: streamValidateUTF8
steps.detail: Called once per non-ASCII run — a run the string scan already flagged from a load it had already paid for — so an ASCII-only document never reaches this function at all.

steps.title: the last three bytes
steps.detail: The block test sees a lead and never the continuation that is missing past the end of the run, so the last three bytes are checked against what may legally sit there before any block runs.

next.label: arm64
next.when: The table lookup exists.

next.label: no byte-table lookup

steps.title: one reduction for the whole run

steps.title: any lane non-zero?

nodes.title: The greedy scan
prose: A number is the one token whose first byte belongs to the token itself, so the structural run hands the byte back rather than consuming it. From there the scan is greedy: take everything that could be part of a number, then decide what shape it was.

The terminator search uses the same fused movemask as the string scan, and it is the row where that change paid most — floats gained 17.6%. It is also the row that pins the limit: one-to-three-digit tokens lose 7.5% to *any* movemask spelling, because the per-lane ladder's moves issue in parallel with the loop test while a movemask makes the lane strictly serial. Three separate variants confirmed no formulation beats the ladder there.

steps.detail: A number is the one token the parser copies rather than borrows, because its bytes have to be joined across the boundary before they can be parsed. A document that ends inside a number is settled by `finish()`.

steps.title: decide what shape it was
steps.detail: Sign, integer digits, fraction, exponent — walked once, in order, over bytes already known to be in the class. The result is a `NumberInfo`: the digits with the dot removed, the power of ten they are scaled by, and the flags a destination needs to reject a value its type cannot hold.

nodes.title: Eight bytes, backwards
prose: An unsigned integer of one to eight digits is parsed whole, with no loop and no data-dependent branch. The digit test doubles as the shape test, so this *replaces* the structured walk's sign, dot and exponent checks for the tokens it accepts rather than adding to them.

The load is the eight bytes *ending* at the token, not starting at it. Those bytes are behind the cursor — already-consumed input in the same buffer — so a single `end >= 8` test makes the read safe, where reading forward would need a bound the parser does not carry. Right alignment also removes the scaling step: the masked-off bytes below the token become leading zeros, so the digit tree's answer is already the value.

The mask must come before the bias. Subtracting `0x30` from the whole word borrows out of any byte below `'0'` — newline, comma and quote all qualify — and into the token's leading digit, so `582` preceded by a newline reads as `482`. nodes.title: StreamParseSink
prose: The parser's whole output surface: one method per token class, each carrying a borrowed `Span<UInt8>` that is invalid the moment the call returns. It is format-agnostic rather than JSON-specific, so another parser could drive the same sinks.

No method throws. A check after every call sits on the hottest path — measured at 2–5% — so a sink records its failure and the parser polls it at token boundaries instead, reporting the failure at the token that provoked it. Sinks record a bool from their apply members rather than throwing, which is what distinguishes a key the destination doesn't have (ignored) from a field that cannot hold this kind of value (a type mismatch).

There is exactly one form per token. A key is always whole; a string always arrives as begin/chunks/end, or as one call when it is complete and escape-free in the chunk. The collapsed forms both protocols once declared are gone — one because no parser could keep the promise, the other because in two rounds of parser work nothing ever called it.

prose: A key is always delivered whole — unescaped, validated UTF-8 — and matching it against a schema's members does not use a `Dictionary`. Keys are compared as precomputed 64-bit words, which for the overwhelming majority of real keys means one or two compares.

prose: A schema describes how a type's members map onto tokens. It is a reference rather than a value, and frames borrow it `unowned(unsafe)` — a retain and release per container open was showing up in the profile.

nodes.title: PartialSink
prose: The typed layer's sink: it keeps a spine of frames, each pointing into the partially built value, and turns tokens into stores. A container entry is now the frame itself — bits rather than references — and scalars whose kind is known at schema-build time are stored directly instead of going through a general applier.

Six codegen traps are recorded against this file. Among them: a struct nested inside the generic sink lowers to a value-witness destroy; `init(rawValue:)` on a decoded enum is not free; and a `count <= 8` branch causes the scan behind it to unroll.

steps.title: a container opens: push a frame
steps.detail: A `BorrowedFrame` is storage, an `unowned(unsafe)` schema, the pending field and a packed route word — 24 bytes. It is trivial, so pushing and popping is a store and a decrement rather than an ARC pair, and deinitializing the stack is a no-op. The storage pointer is the load-bearing part: only the innermost open container is ever mutated, so an element pointer stays valid for that element's lifetime — appending to an outer array cannot happen while an inner one is open — and a copy of the value taken *between* parse calls cannot invalidate one either, because every container holds its open element inline at a fixed offset in storage the stream owns, so the copy diverges and the address the frame holds still names the parser's own element.

nodes.title: StreamString
prose: Bytes accumulate; producing a `String` is a read, not a side effect. Storage grows in blocks whose size doubles, so a long streamed string does not pay a reallocation per chunk.

In the allocation census the block ramp was the smaller half of the cost. The larger sources were the bookkeeping array tracking the blocks and a tail reserve on the fragment-fed path. Fixing those measured +11.2% on the LLM message and +5.5% on GSoC.

The accumulated bytes are also readable as the words a generated matcher compares, which is what lets `@StreamParseable` on a raw-`String` enum emit the same shape of matcher for a case name that it emits for an object key.

steps.detail: `String.streamAppend` is `self += String(decoding:)` — a whole intermediate `String` built and destroyed per chunk, re-validating UTF-8 the parser already validated, ~61 ns per content byte under byte-fed input.

steps.title: StreamInlineString
steps.detail: A fixed-capacity string whose storage the parser appends into directly, for a member that declares its own ceiling.

steps.title: promoteSizedInlineStorage
steps.detail: The first overflow sizes the schedule's start: a value that arrives as one big span starts on a block matched to half its size instead of walking the whole doubling ramp, while a fragment-fed value keeps the 512-byte start and lets the ramp absorb growth. Outlined, because promotion happens once per value and its body inlined into every `stringChunk` call site is exactly the growth that flips the parse loop's inlining.

steps.title: appendBlocked
steps.detail: Fill the tail, seal it, start the next. The physical layout can differ between hinted, unhinted and differently-fed values, so every physical boundary is a multiple of 512 and reads, equality, ordering and hashing use canonical 512-byte logical windows.

steps.title: reserve the block, not the fragment
steps.detail: An empty tail reserving only what the fragment needs is right for the *first* block and wrong for every one after it: a seal empties the tail, so a fragment-fed value re-entered that arm at every block and grew in 512-byte steps, paying a reallocation per block. Escape-split values are exactly the ones that hit it. LLM message +11.2%, GSoC +5.5%.

next.label: the fragment fit

steps.title: blocks.append(tail); capacity <<= 1
steps.detail: Doubling, capped at 8 KiB. `blocks` reserves four up front, because it grew by doubling from its first append and a three-block value paid two array reallocations for a spine that was the *other* larger half of the census.

steps.detail: The schedule is a pure function of the first block's shift and the block index, so locating a byte stays closed form rather than a search over prefix sums.

steps.title: producing a String is a read
steps.detail: Bytes accumulate; decoding happens once, when someone asks. Accumulating raw bytes and decoding at read was the floor the append benchmarks found, ~7× under the append path at small chunks.

steps.title: paddedWord, then isPrefix
steps.kicker: the read side of the key encoding
steps.detail: The same little-endian, zero-padded eight-byte encoding a key span produces, read back out of the accumulated bytes — so a generated matcher compares an accumulated value against a compile-time literal with the identical codegen it already uses for object keys: a `switch` on the leading word, a count check, then any remaining words. The count check is not optional, because an accumulated value may hold a decoded NUL and the padding is otherwise indistinguishable from one. Unlike a key span, whose bytes are a borrow into the document with more document behind them, an accumulated value's last block ends where the value does, so the window is clamped rather than overread. `isPrefix(of:)` is the direction a *streaming* match needs and the mirror of `hasPrefix`: whether what has arrived so far is still consistent with a case name, not whether the name has already arrived. A matcher walks its cases shortest-first asking it, and declines outright on zero bytes — an empty accumulation is a prefix of every case, so answering would be a definite answer on no evidence that then changes as the real bytes land.

nodes.title: Arrays and dictionaries
prose: Streaming collections with their own storage. Closed elements live in uniform power-of-two blocks the value shares by retaining rather than copying, and the one element the parser is still writing lives inline, outside them.

The dictionary's index is a single table with one entry buffer; `Dictionary` was measured against it and lost outright. Both structural guesses made when designing that table turned out to be wrong, and one of them has since been reversed again — the values are blocked now.

Moving the open element into the blocks was built, measured and reverted. What stayed is the block type it needed, which turned out to buy something larger: a shared block is written past rather than copied, so the commit path has no copy-on-write check on it at all.

nodes.invokes: Streaming storage with its own index: a single table with one entry buffer, measured against `Dictionary` and faster.

steps.title: the open element lives outside the storage
steps.detail: `pending` is held inline, so the parser's frame points at a slot no other value can see and its address survives every append — and a plain copy of the value diverges it for free, with no allocation and no bookkeeping, which is the whole reason a snapshot is a struct copy. Opening the element in the storage instead was built and measured: it bought a third on the largest partials and cost 59–72% on every row that *keeps* a snapshot, because the divergence then has to be bought back with a heap block per retained snapshot.

next.label: an array element closed
next.when: The frame's destination is a `StreamArray`, so the pending element is committed into the filling block.

next.label: a dictionary value closed
next.when: The frame's destination is a `StreamDictionary`, whose slot was opened when the key arrived rather than now.

steps.title: commit into the filling block
steps.detail: Closed elements live in uniform power-of-two blocks, and each array holds its *own* count of the ones in the filling block, captured by value when the array is copied. A snapshot's elements are therefore a prefix of the filling block's, and the parser appends above that prefix — memory no snapshot reads — so there is no copy-on-write check on the commit path at all, at any block size. Only a write *into* the prefix copies, and copies one block: the checked subscript, or a repeated dictionary key landing in a sealed one. A power of two means the sealed count is `blocks.count << shift` and needs no stored field.

next.label: and that is already a snapshot

steps.title: StreamBlock
steps.detail: A `ManagedBuffer` with the elements tail-allocated, not a `ContiguousArray`. An array never exposes its spare capacity, so committing meant handing the element to `append` and letting the array copy it in — and a shared array copies *all* of its elements before the first of those writes. Owning the capacity outright is what lets the parser write the element into the slot it will live in, and what lets a shared block be written past. One object rather than two: the two-allocation form doubled the malloc count of every number-heavy corpus (Canada 2,659 → 5,109) and cost them 10–28%. The header is read through its pointer rather than as a stored class property, which from outside its module is a dynamic `swift_beginAccess` even in release, and it is deliberately not generic over the element, because a generic header makes the elements' offset a metadata question wherever the block is reached unspecialised — 7–8% on GitHub and GSoC.

steps.title: one entry buffer, one slot table
steps.detail: Byte-keyed slots rather than a `[String: Int]`: 12 to 17 ns per hit against 34 to 42, flat in key count, and no allocation on a lookup where a `Dictionary` materialises a `String` for one. `pendingSlot` is an existing slot when the key repeats, which is what keeps `{"a":1,"b":2,"a":3}` in its original order.

and that is already a snapshot

steps.title: blocking cost 2×; one buffer beat two
steps.detail: Both structural guesses made when designing that table were wrong. Blocking the storage the way the array does cost 2× on the discarding path, because a dictionary reads its storage back on every lookup where an array never reads at all. And a retained state's cost tracks the *number* of buffers it shares, not their size, so the key and its hash travel together and the table is one array rather than a heads-and-next pair.

steps.title: the values are blocked too
steps.detail: `storedValues` is a `StreamArray`, for the reason the elements are: a snapshot shares the blocks instead of copying them. That reverses one of the two guesses above — a flat `[Value]` makes a snapshot-per-byte parse copy the whole value array per byte, measured at 58% off the dictionary snapshot rows, and the 2× finding had no snapshot row in front of it. The dictionary still keeps its *own* open value rather than borrowing the array's, because a repeated key's open value is an element the array already holds, and unlike an append a write into one of those is a write a kept state can see. That write happens inside the drain, with the block it lands in made unique first, so no state can be taken between the check and the write.

steps.title: a plain value copy
steps.detail: Everything left of the parse cursor is immutable, so copying the value retains the blocks rather than copying them — which is why nothing here has a `streamSnapshot()`. The one thing the copy has to diverge is the element the parser is still inside, and holding that inline diverges it for free. `Sendable` is asserted rather than checked here, because the blocks are objects: what makes sharing one safe is the rule that it is only ever written above the count every sharer captured, not the type system.

nodes.title: Views and snapshots
prose: Reading a partially parsed value costs what is read. Every parseable type has a `~Copyable`, `~Escapable` view — in practice a typed pointer into the value — that cannot outlive the call that lent it, so reading a field does not copy the document.

Snapshots are the alternative: the async sequence conveniences take a full one per element, because an escaping value has to own its storage. The freeze-the-completed-prefix work is what reduced their cost.

steps.detail: In practice a typed pointer into the value. It is `~Copyable` and `~Escapable` and arrives borrowed, so the compiler ties it to the call that produced it and there is no way to store it — where the old `View == Self` default trusted a caller not to move it elsewhere.
